stem_html: A taxi charges a fixed pickup fee plus a constant rate per kilometre. A 6 km trip costs \$15.00 and a 15 km trip costs \$33.00. What is the cost, in dollars, of a 10 km trip?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A fixed fee breaks proportionality. Doubling the distance does not double the fare.
  • Two unknowns, two given trips. The rate comes from the difference and the fee from either point.
  • Forgetting the fee at the last step is the most common single slip.

Why A is right The rate is \(\dfrac{33-15}{15-6}=\dfrac{18}{9}=2\) dollars per kilometre, so the fee is \(15-6(2)=3\). A 10 km trip costs \(3+10(2)=23\).

Why B is wrong 22 uses the rate alone, \(10\times 2\), plus a fee of 2. The fee is 3, and it has to be found from one of the given trips.

Why C is wrong 25 scales 15.00 by \(\dfrac{10}{6}\), which treats the cost as directly proportional to distance. A fixed fee makes it not proportional.

Why D is wrong 20 is \(10\times 2\) with the fee left out entirely.

stem_html:
\(\dfrac{3}{x-2}=\dfrac{5}{x+6}\)

What is the solution to the given equation?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Which numerator multiplies which denominator. Cross-multiplication pairs each numerator with the opposite denominator.
  • Collecting \(x\) on the correct side. \(3x-5x\) and \(5x-3x\) differ by a sign.
  • Substituting back takes ten seconds and rules out three of the four.

Why A is right Cross-multiplying gives \(3(x+6)=5(x-2)\), so \(3x+18=5x-10\), \(28=2x\) and \(x=14\). Checking, \(\dfrac{3}{12}=\dfrac{5}{20}=\dfrac14\).

Why B is wrong \(-14\) comes from \(2x=-28\), which is what happens when the two sides are subtracted in the wrong order at the last step.

Why C is wrong 4 comes from cross-multiplying the numerators against the wrong denominators, \(3(x-2)=5(x+6)\), which gives \(-36=2x\) and not 4; it is also what a student reaches by setting \(x-2\) and \(x+6\) proportional to 3 and 5 in the wrong order.

Why D is wrong \(-4\) makes the left denominator \(-6\) and the right denominator 2, giving \(-\dfrac12\) and \(\dfrac52\), which are not equal.

stem_html: The line \(y=g(x)\) passes through \((-3,10)\) and \((5,-6)\). For what value of \(x\) does \(g(x)=0\)?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • \(g(x)=0\) against \(g(0)\). The two are different questions and both answers are among the choices.
  • The slope is negative, and every intermediate number in this problem appears as a choice.
  • Two negatives in the denominator. \(5-(-3)=8\).

Why A is right The slope is \(\dfrac{-6-10}{5-(-3)}=\dfrac{-16}{8}=-2\), so \(y-10=-2(x+3)\) and \(y=-2x+4\). Setting \(y=0\) gives \(x=2\).

Why B is wrong 4 is the \(y\)-intercept, the value of \(g(0)\). The question asks where the output is 0, not what the output is at 0.

Why C is wrong \(-2\) is the slope. It is the number computed first and it is not an \(x\)-intercept.

Why D is wrong 0 is the output being set, not the input that produces it.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
stem_html:
\(\begin{aligned} 6x-4y &= 10 \\ -3x+2y &= k \end{aligned}\)

In the given system, \(k\) is a constant. For what value of \(k\) does the system have infinitely many solutions?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The scale factor is negative. \(-3\) times \(-2\) is 6.
  • Infinitely many solutions means identical equations, not merely parallel ones — parallel with different constants gives no solution.
  • Numbers already in the system are offered as choices.

Why A is right Multiplying the second equation by \(-2\) gives \(6x-4y=-2k\). The system has infinitely many solutions when the two equations are the same, so \(-2k=10\) and \(k=-5\).

Why B is wrong 5 is \(10\div 2\) with the sign of the multiplier ignored. The second equation has to be scaled by \(-2\), not by 2, to match the first.

Why C is wrong 10 is the constant in the first equation. The two equations have different coefficients, so they cannot share the same constant.

Why D is wrong \(-10\) multiplies 10 by \(-1\) instead of dividing by \(-2\).

skill: Linear inequalities in one or two variables
stem_html:
\(-3x+7 \ge 4x-14\)

Which inequality gives all values of \(x\) that satisfy the given inequality?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Dividing by a negative reverses the symbol. Moving the \(x\) terms to the side that keeps the coefficient positive avoids the issue entirely.
  • Reading \(3\ge x\) off the page. The variable is on the right, so the symbol looks reversed.
  • Signs when constants cross the inequality.

Why A is right Adding \(3x\) and 14 to both sides gives \(21\ge 7x\), so \(3\ge x\), that is \(x\le 3\).

Why B is wrong The inequality symbol has been copied rather than read. \(3\ge x\) says 3 is at least \(x\), which is \(x\le 3\).

Why C is wrong Moving the \(x\) terms to the left instead gives \(-7x\ge -21\), and dividing by \(-7\) requires reversing the symbol. Keeping it gives \(x\ge 3\) written as \(x\le -3\) after a further sign slip.

Why D is wrong \(-1\) comes from \(7-14=-7\) divided by 7, which mishandles the constants: the \(-14\) moves to the left as \(+14\).

stem_html: The graph of \(4x+ky=12\) in the \(xy\)-plane has an \(x\)-intercept at \((3,0)\) and passes through \((0,-4)\). What is the value of \(k\)?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Which point to use. The \(x\)-intercept contains no \(y\), so it cannot determine \(k\).
  • Sign of the \(y\)-coordinate.
  • Division the right way up. \(k=12/(-4)\).

Why A is right Substituting \((0,-4)\) gives \(4(0)+k(-4)=12\), so \(-4k=12\) and \(k=-3\). The \(x\)-intercept is automatically satisfied: \(4(3)=12\).

Why B is wrong 3 solves \(4k=12\), which is what comes of substituting \(y=4\) rather than \(y=-4\).

Why C is wrong \(-4\) is the \(y\)-coordinate of the given point, not the coefficient.

Why D is wrong \(-\dfrac13\) inverts the division, using \(\dfrac{-4}{12}\) instead of \(\dfrac{12}{-4}\).

stem_html: A candle burns at a constant rate. After 3 hours it is 21 cm tall and after 7 hours it is 13 cm tall. How tall was the candle before it was lit?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • How far back to extend. From \(t=3\) to \(t=0\) is three hours, not the four between the two readings.
  • The rate is negative, so going backwards in time adds height.
  • The rate itself is offered as an answer.

Why A is right The rate is \(\dfrac{13-21}{7-3}=-2\) cm per hour, so the height is \(h(t)=21-2(t-3)=27-2t\) and \(h(0)=27\).

Why B is wrong 24 subtracts one hour's burn too few, using \(21+2(3)-3\) or extending back only two hours instead of three.

Why C is wrong 29 extends back with the wrong number of hours, adding \(2\times 4\) to 21 because 4 is the gap between the two given times.

Why D is wrong 2 is the burn rate in centimetres per hour with its sign removed.

stem_html:
\(x^{2}+kx+36=0\)

In the given equation, \(k\) is a constant. If the equation has exactly one real solution, what is the greatest possible value of \(k\)?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two values of \(k\) satisfy the condition, and the question asks for one of them by name.
  • Stopping at \(k^{2}\).
  • The repeated root is a value of \(x\) and is easy to report instead.

Why A is right Exactly one real solution means the discriminant is zero: \(k^{2}-4(1)(36)=0\), so \(k^{2}=144\) and \(k=\pm 12\). The greatest of these is 12.

Why B is wrong \(-12\) is the other root of \(k^{2}=144\) and is the least of the two values, not the greatest.

Why C is wrong 6 is the solution of the equation when \(k=-12\): \(x^{2}-12x+36=(x-6)^{2}\). It is a value of \(x\), not of \(k\).

Why D is wrong 144 is \(k^{2}\). One square root remains.

stem_html: Which expression is equivalent to \((2x-3)^{2}-(x+4)^{2}\)?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The minus sign in front of the second square applies to all three of its terms.
  • Squaring a coefficient. \((2x)^{2}\) is \(4x^{2}\).
  • Two of the wrong answers get the \(x\) term right and lose the constant.

Why A is right \((2x-3)^{2}=4x^{2}-12x+9\) and \((x+4)^{2}=x^{2}+8x+16\). Subtracting, \(4x^{2}-12x+9-x^{2}-8x-16=3x^{2}-20x-7\).

Why B is wrong This subtracts \(8x\) as though it were positive on both sides: \(-12x+8x=-4x\). The whole second square is subtracted, so \(+8x\) becomes \(-8x\).

Why C is wrong This subtracts the \(x\) terms correctly and then adds the constants, \(9+16=25\), instead of subtracting.

Why D is wrong This treats \((2x-3)^{2}\) as \(2x^{2}-\dots\), squaring only the \(x\) and not the coefficient. \((2x)^{2}=4x^{2}\).

stem_html: The function \(h\) is defined by \(h(x)=x^{2}-8x+7\). For what value of \(x\) is \(h(x)\) at its minimum, and what is that minimum?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • \(-\dfrac{b}{2a}\) with a negative \(b\). The two minus signs cancel.
  • Dividing by \(2a\), not by \(a\).
  • The constant term is the value at 0, not the minimum.

Why A is right The vertex is at \(x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}=\dfrac{8}{2}=4\), and \(h(4)=16-32+7=-9\).

Why B is wrong \(-4\) drops the minus sign in \(-\dfrac{b}{2a}\) when \(b\) is already negative. Two negatives make the vertex positive.

Why C is wrong 7 is \(h(0)\), the \(y\)-intercept. The minimum is the output at the vertex, not at zero.

Why D is wrong 8 is \(|b|\) rather than \(-\dfrac{b}{2a}\), and 7 is again the intercept.

stem_html: A ball is thrown upward from a platform. Its height, in metres, after \(t\) seconds is \(H(t)=-5t^{2}+20t+25\). How many seconds after it is thrown does the ball reach its greatest height?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Time against height. Both the peak time and the peak height are among the choices, and only one carries seconds.
  • Landing time is a different vertex-adjacent number and is easy to compute by accident.
  • The constant term is the starting height.

Why A is right The vertex is at \(t=-\dfrac{20}{2(-5)}=2\) seconds.

Why B is wrong 5 is when the ball lands: \(-5t^{2}+20t+25=0\) factors as \(-5(t-5)(t+1)\). That is the end of the flight, not its peak.

Why C is wrong 45 is the greatest height, \(H(2)\), in metres. The question asks for a time.

Why D is wrong 25 is the height at \(t=0\), the height of the platform.

stem_html: If \(a>0\) and \(b>0\), which expression is equivalent to \(\dfrac{\left(a^{3}b^{-2}\right)^{2}}{a^{4}b^{-5}}\)?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Division subtracts exponents; multiplication adds them. Both operations appear here.
  • Subtracting a negative exponent. \(-4-(-5)=+1\).
  • The outer exponent multiplies. \((a^{3})^{2}=a^{6}\).

Why A is right The numerator is \(a^{6}b^{-4}\). Dividing, \(a^{6-4}=a^{2}\) and \(b^{-4-(-5)}=b^{1}\), so the expression is \(a^{2}b\).

Why B is wrong \(-9\) comes from \(-4+(-5)\), adding the exponents of \(b\) instead of subtracting. Division subtracts.

Why C is wrong \(a^{10}\) adds the exponents of \(a\), \(6+4\), instead of subtracting them.

Why D is wrong \(b^{9}\) subtracts in the wrong order, \(-5-(-4)\) negated, and loses the sign twice.

stem_html:
\(\dfrac{x}{x-3}+\dfrac{2}{x}=\dfrac{9}{x^{2}-3x}\)

What is the solution to the given equation?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Clearing denominators can invent a root. The excluded value is exactly the one that makes a denominator zero.
  • The excluded value is visible before any algebra. \(x\neq 0\) and \(x\neq 3\) can be written down at the start.
  • Sign of the surviving root. \((x+5)\) gives \(x=-5\).

Why A is right Multiplying by \(x(x-3)\) gives \(x^{2}+2(x-3)=9\), so \(x^{2}+2x-15=0\) and \(x=-5\) or \(x=3\). Since \(x=3\) makes a denominator zero it is excluded, leaving \(x=-5\). Checking: \(\dfrac{-5}{-8}+\dfrac{2}{-5}=\dfrac{25-16}{40}=\dfrac{9}{40}\), and \(x^{2}-3x=25+15=40\).

Why B is wrong \(x=3\) makes \(x-3=0\) and \(x^{2}-3x=0\), so two of the three fractions are undefined. It is a root of the cleared equation and not of the original one.

Why C is wrong 5 is \(-5\) with the sign lost; \(x^{2}+2x-15\) factors as \((x+5)(x-3)\), so the root is \(-5\).

Why D is wrong Reporting both roots keeps the excluded one. Clearing denominators can create solutions, and each candidate has to be checked against the original denominators.

stem_html: The function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x)=3^{x}\). If \(g(x)=f(x+2)\), which expression is equivalent to \(g(x)\)?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Inside the function against outside it. \(f(x+2)\) and \(f(x)+2\) do different things.
  • Exponent rules turn a shift into a factor. \(3^{x+2}=3^{x}3^{2}\).
  • \(3^{2}\) is 9, not 6.

Why A is right \(g(x)=3^{x+2}=3^{x}\cdot 3^{2}=9\cdot 3^{x}\). A horizontal shift of an exponential is a vertical stretch.

Why B is wrong Adding 9 is a vertical shift, which is what \(f(x)+9\) would be. Replacing \(x\) with \(x+2\) changes the input, not the output.

Why C is wrong 6 is \(3\times 2\), multiplying the base by the shift instead of raising the base to it.

Why D is wrong \(3^{2x}\) is \(f(2x)\), a horizontal compression rather than a shift.

stem_html: A store's revenue in 2023 was 20 percent higher than in 2022, and its revenue in 2024 was 25 percent lower than in 2023. The 2024 revenue was what percent of the 2022 revenue?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Percentages of different bases do not add. 20 is of 2022 and 25 is of 2023.
  • Multiply the factors. \(1.20\times0.75=0.90\).
  • The order does not matter for the product, but the base for each step does.

Why A is right Taking 2022 as 100, 2023 is 120 and 2024 is \(120\times 0.75=90\). So 2024 is 90 percent of 2022.

Why B is wrong 95 comes from \(100+20-25\), adding and subtracting the percentages directly. The 25 percent is taken of 120, not of 100.

Why C is wrong 105 applies the decrease first and the increase second in the wrong proportion, or subtracts 25 from 120 and then adds 10.

Why D is wrong 85 subtracts 25 percent of 100 from 120 minus 10, mixing bases again. No consistent computation produces it.

stem_html: A bag contains 5 red marbles and 7 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Without replacement” changes the second fraction twice — 4 reds left out of 11 marbles.
  • Squaring is the with-replacement answer and is very close to the right one numerically.
  • Doubling instead of multiplying.

Why A is right The first draw is red with probability \(\dfrac{5}{12}\); given that, the second is red with probability \(\dfrac{4}{11}\). The product is \(\dfrac{20}{132}=\dfrac{5}{33}\).

Why B is wrong \(\left(\dfrac{5}{12}\right)^{2}\) treats the draws as independent, which they are only with replacement. Removing the first marble changes both numerator and denominator.

Why C is wrong \(\dfrac{5}{12}\) is the probability the first marble is red. It is one factor of the answer.

Why D is wrong \(\dfrac{10}{12}\) doubles the numerator, treating two draws as twice the chance. Probabilities of joint events multiply, they do not add.

skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
stem_html: A recipe that serves 8 requires 300 mL of stock. A cook wants to serve 20 and has 700 mL of stock. How many additional millilitres of stock are needed?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Total against shortfall. The last subtraction is the step the question actually asks for.
  • Which way the ratio goes. More servings means more stock.
  • Two plausible subtractions. Subtracting 300 answers a different question.

Why A is right Serving 20 needs \(300\times\dfrac{20}{8}=750\) mL. With 700 mL on hand, \(750-700=50\) mL more are needed.

Why B is wrong 750 is the total required, not the shortfall. The 700 mL already available has to be subtracted.

Why C is wrong 450 is \(300\times\dfrac{20}{8}-300\), the extra above one batch rather than the extra above what the cook has.

Why D is wrong 120 uses \(\dfrac{8}{20}\) instead of \(\dfrac{20}{8}\), scaling the recipe down when it needs scaling up.

stem_html: A model predicts a town's population as \(P=1{,}800(1.04)^{t}\), where \(t\) is the number of years after 2010. Which statement best describes what the model says about the population?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "It increases by 4 percent each year."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "It increases by 4 people each year.", "trap": "unit-mismatch"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "It increases by 104 people each year.", "trap": "unit-mismatch"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "It increases by 1,800 people every 4 years.", "trap": "shortcut-trap"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A base is a ratio, not a count.
  • Exponential against linear. Constant percent, not constant amount.
  • Each number in the model has a role, and three of the choices give one of them the wrong one.

Why A is right In \(P=P_{0}(1+r)^{t}\) the base \(1.04\) is \(1+r\) with \(r=0.04\), which is a 4 percent increase per year.

Why B is wrong A constant increase of 4 people a year would be the linear model \(P=1800+4t\). An exponent produces a constant ratio, not a constant difference.

Why C is wrong 104 reads the base as a number of people. It is a multiplier, and 1.04 multiplied by any population gives a growth that depends on the population.

Why D is wrong 1,800 is the population in 2010, the initial value, and the 4 in the base is not a number of years.

skill: One-variable data: Distributions and measures of center and spread
stem_html: Two data sets each contain 6 values. Set A is \(\{4,5,6,6,7,8\}\) and set B is \(\{1,3,6,6,9,11\}\). Which statement is true?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "The two sets have the same mean and set B has the greater standard deviation."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "The two sets have the same mean and the same standard deviation.", "trap": "mean-vs-median"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Set B has the greater mean and the greater standard deviation.", "trap": "mean-vs-median"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Set A has the greater mean and set B has the greater standard deviation.", "trap": "mean-vs-median"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A wider spread looks like a larger centre. Adding the values is the only way to check.
  • Both sets share the middle two values, so the median is the same too.
  • Equal means, unequal spreads is the whole point of the pair.

Why A is right Both sets sum to 36, so both means are 6. Set B's values sit farther from 6 than set A's do, so B has the greater standard deviation.

Why B is wrong The spreads differ: set A ranges from 4 to 8 and set B from 1 to 11. Equal means do not imply equal spreads.

Why C is wrong Both means are 6. The larger values in set B are balanced by its smaller ones.

Why D is wrong Set A's mean is not greater; the two sums are identical at 36.

stem_html: A survey of 400 households found that 140 own a bicycle. Of those, 35 own more than one. What percentage of the households surveyed own exactly one bicycle?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Which count and which total. Every wrong choice is a real ratio from the same three numbers.
  • “Exactly one” requires a subtraction before any division.
  • The denominator is 400, because the question says “of the households surveyed.”

Why A is right Exactly one is \(140-35=105\) households, and \(\dfrac{105}{400}=0.2625\), or 26.25 percent.

Why B is wrong 25 percent is \(\dfrac{35}{140}\), the fraction of bicycle owners with more than one. The question asks for a percentage of all 400 households.

Why C is wrong 35 percent is \(\dfrac{140}{400}\), the fraction owning any bicycle at all, which includes the 35 with more than one.

Why D is wrong 8.75 percent is \(\dfrac{35}{400}\), the fraction owning more than one.

stem_html: In a class of 30 students, 18 study Latin, 14 study Greek, and 5 study neither. How many students study both?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The union is not the class. Five students belong to neither set.
  • Adding the two counts double-counts the overlap, which is what makes the subtraction necessary.
  • Every wrong choice comes from using 30 where 25 belongs.

Why A is right Students studying at least one language number \(30-5=25\). By inclusion and exclusion, \(18+14-\text{both}=25\), so both \(=32-25=7\).

Why B is wrong 4 subtracts 5 from the overlap or uses 30 rather than 25 as the union: \(18+14-30=2\) and adjusting by 2 gives 4. The union is 25.

Why C is wrong 32 is \(18+14\), which double-counts every student taking both languages.

Why D is wrong 2 is \(18+14-30\), which uses the whole class as the union and ignores the 5 who study neither.

stem_html: In a circle of radius 9, a central angle of \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\) radians subtends an arc. What is the length of that arc?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Arc length against sector area. Both are natural things to compute and only one is a length.
  • Radians make the formula multiplicative. No degree conversion is needed.
  • The angle alone is the arc length on the unit circle only.

Why A is right Arc length is \(r\theta\) with \(\theta\) in radians: \(9\cdot\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=6\pi\).

Why B is wrong \(27\pi\) is the area of the sector, \(\dfrac12 r^{2}\theta=\dfrac12\cdot 81\cdot\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=27\pi\). It is an area, not a length.

Why C is wrong \(3\pi\) divides by the radius instead of multiplying, using \(\dfrac{\theta}{r}\) scaled up.

Why D is wrong \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\) is the angle itself, which is the arc length only in a circle of radius 1.

stem_html: In triangle \(DEF\), angle \(E\) is a right angle, \(DE=8\), and \(\tan D=\dfrac{3}{4}\). What is the length of \(DF\)?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Which leg is opposite \(D\). With the right angle at \(E\), the side opposite \(D\) is \(EF\).
  • The intermediate leg is offered as an answer.
  • The hypotenuse is not the sum of the legs.

Why A is right With the right angle at \(E\), \(\tan D=\dfrac{EF}{DE}=\dfrac{EF}{8}=\dfrac{3}{4}\), so \(EF=6\). Then \(DF=\sqrt{8^{2}+6^{2}}=10\).

Why B is wrong 6 is \(EF\), the leg found on the way. \(DF\) is the hypotenuse.

Why C is wrong \(\dfrac{32}{3}\) uses \(\tan D=\dfrac{DE}{EF}\), inverting opposite and adjacent.

Why D is wrong 14 adds the two legs, \(8+6\), instead of using the Pythagorean theorem.

stem_html: A cone and a cylinder have the same radius and the same height. The cylinder's volume is \(96\pi\) cubic centimetres. What is the cone's volume, in cubic centimetres?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • One third, not one half. The half applies to a triangle against a rectangle, not to a cone against a cylinder.
  • Direction of the factor. A cone holds less.
  • No radius or height is needed, which makes the ratio the whole problem.

Why A is right A cone is one third of the cylinder with the same base and height, so the volume is \(\dfrac{96\pi}{3}=32\pi\).

Why B is wrong \(48\pi\) halves the cylinder. The factor is a third, not a half.

Why C is wrong \(288\pi\) multiplies by 3 instead of dividing.

Why D is wrong \(24\pi\) divides by 4, which is the factor relating areas rather than volumes.

stem_html: Triangle \(ABC\) is similar to triangle \(DEF\), with \(A\) corresponding to \(D\). If \(AB=6\), \(DE=15\), and the area of triangle \(ABC\) is 20 square units, what is the area of triangle \(DEF\), in square units?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Areas scale by the square of the ratio. Applying the ratio once is the commonest error on similar figures.
  • Which figure is larger. \(DE>AB\), so the area grows.
  • Volumes would scale by the cube, and the same trap appears there.

Why A is right The linear scale factor is \(\dfrac{15}{6}=\dfrac{5}{2}\), so areas scale by \(\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{25}{4}\). The area is \(20\cdot\dfrac{25}{4}=125\).

Why B is wrong 50 applies the linear factor \(\dfrac{5}{2}\) directly to the area. Area scales by the square of the linear factor.

Why C is wrong 8 applies \(\dfrac{2}{5}\), scaling the wrong way: \(DEF\) is the larger triangle.

Why D is wrong 32 applies \(\dfrac{4}{25}\) inverted and rounded, again scaling down.
